dataset.what_one_row_represents: One Sechselaeuten festival year - the Boeoegg burn duration (minutes) plus that year's June-August summer climate measurements from MeteoSwiss for the Swiss Plateau
dataset.time_range: 1923 to 2025 (sparse pre-1952, near-complete after 1952; 2 NA durations - 2020 cancelled by COVID, 2024 cancelled by storm)

ana_01.label: Dataset profile and missingness
ana_01.content: The dataset has 67 rows spanning 1923 to 2025, with 9 columns: festival year, Boeoegg burn duration in minutes, and six MeteoSwiss climate variables for the Swiss Plateau summer (mean, min, max temperature; total sunshine; sunshine percentage of possible; total precipitation), plus a record flag for summers with mean >= 19 deg C. Only the duration column has missing values, with two NAs - 2020 (COVID-19 cancellation) and 2024 (cancelled because of stormy weather). All 67 climate observations are present. The series is sparse before 1952 (only 1923 is recorded between 1923 and 1951), then near-complete from 1952 onward. The non-null duration count is 65.

rows: 67
columns: ['year', 'duration', 'tre200m0', 'tre200mn', 'tre200mx', 'sre000m0', 'sremaxmv', 'rre150m0', 'record']
year range: 1923 to 2025
years with NA duration: [2020, 2024]
non-null duration rows: 65

ana_02.label: Boeoegg burn-duration distribution
ana_02.content: Across 65 recorded burns, the duration ranges from 4.00 to 60.00 minutes, with a mean of 17.64 min and a median of just 13.00 min - the distribution is right-skewed because most burns end fairly fast and only a handful drag on past 30 minutes. The standard deviation is 11.87 min. Quartiles: 25% of burns are under 10 minutes, 50% are under 13, 75% are under 23.5, and 90% finish within 32 minutes. Histogram bins (in minutes) show 1 burn under 5, 15 burns 5-10, 19 burns 10-15, 7 burns 15-20, 11 burns 20-25, 5 burns 25-30, 2 burns 30-40, and 5 burns 40-60.

data_table.description: Histogram of burn durations across 65 recorded years

ana_03.label: Extremes - shortest and longest burns
ana_03.content: The shortest five burns are 4.00 min (1956), 5.00 (1971), 5.00 (1968), 5.12 (1974) and 5.70 (2003). The longest five are 40.00 (1988), 40.00 (1970), 43.57 (2016), 57.00 (2023) and 60.00 (1923). Of the five fastest, only 2003 was a record-hot summer (21.67 deg C); the other four were ordinary. Of the five slowest, only 2023 was a record summer - 57 minutes of smoldering before a 20.07 deg C summer. The two extremes that frame the dataset (1956 at 4 min, 1923 at 60 min) sit on opposite ends of the duration scale but were both followed by below-average summers (15.07 and 16.67 deg C respectively).

data_table.description: Top-5 shortest and top-5 longest burns with that year's mean summer temperature and record flag

ana_04.label: Swiss-Plateau summer temperature distribution
ana_04.content: The summer-mean temperature column spans 15.07 to 21.67 deg C across all 67 years, with mean 17.61 and median 17.50 (sd 1.34). 11 of the 67 summers cross the 19 deg C MeteoSwiss record threshold: 1983, 1994, 2003, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. Note 2024 has no burn duration (the snowman was not lit), so only 10 record summers can be paired with a burn time.

data_table.description: Every record summer (mean >= 19 deg C) with year, summer T, and that year's burn duration (NaN where snowman was cancelled)

ana_05.label: Pearson correlations: burn duration vs each climate variable
ana_05.content: Across 65 paired observations, the Pearson correlation between burn duration and the headline climate variable - summer mean temperature (tre200m0) - is just r = 0.194, with p = 0.121, not statistically significant. The folk rule predicts a NEGATIVE correlation (faster burn = hotter summer); the data shows a weak POSITIVE one (slower burn associates very mildly with hotter summers). The only correlation that reaches conventional significance is duration vs absolute summer maximum temperature (tre200mx) at r = 0.276, p = 0.026, again positive. Sunshine totals (r = 0.168) and sunshine percentage (r = 0.170) are also non-significant; precipitation is r = -0.113 and non-significant. Across all six climate variables, none supports the folk-science direction.

notable_instance.name: tre200m0 - summer mean temperature
notable_instance.why: This is the headline test of the folk claim - and the snowman fails it: the correlation is in the wrong direction and not statistically significant.

ana_06.label: Spearman rank correlations - robustness check
ana_06.content: Spearman rank correlations remove the influence of the dataset's most extreme burns (4 min in 1956, 60 min in 1923, 57 min in 2023). With ranks, the correlation between duration and summer mean temperature drops further to rho = 0.173 (p = 0.168), and the previously significant correlation with summer max (0.276) collapses to rho = 0.169 (p = 0.180). Sunshine correlations vanish (rho = 0.005 and 0.007). The conclusion does not depend on outliers: there is no robust statistical signal in any direction.

data_table.description: Spearman rank correlation (rho) of burn duration with each climate variable

ana_07.label: Folk-rule split test: fast burns vs slow burns
ana_07.content: Splitting the 65 burns at the median (13 min), the folk rule predicts the 32 fast-burn years should be hotter than the 33 slow-burn years. They are not. The fast group's mean summer temperature is 17.49 deg C; the slow group's is 17.64 deg C - a difference of -0.148 deg C in the wrong direction. The Welch t-test gives t = -0.45, p = 0.66, indistinguishable from zero. Just as starkly, only 2 of the 32 fast-burn years (6.3%) were record summers, while 8 of the 33 slow-burn years (24.2%) were. By the only criterion the folk rule cares about, slow burns predict record summers four times more often than fast burns do.

fast burns (n=32): mean summer T = 17.49C, record summers = 2/32

diff in mean T (fast - slow): -0.148C
Welch t-test on mean summer T: t=-0.45, p=0.6571

data_table.description: Comparing fast (<13 min) vs slow (>=13 min) burns

ana_08.label: Folk-rule classification accuracy vs base rate
ana_08.content: Treating fast burns as a folk-rule prediction of a record summer, the confusion matrix shows 25 true negatives, 30 false alarms, 8 misses, and just 2 hits. Total agreement is 27/65 = 41.5%. Critically, the base-rate strategy of always predicting 'no record summer' achieves 55/65 = 84.6% accuracy. The folk rule is roughly half as accurate as just saying nothing - it has informative value below noise.

ana_09.label: Celebrity case studies: famous hits and misses
ana_09.content: The dataset reproduces every example MeteoSwiss cites. 1974 - shortest burn (5.12 min) - was followed by an unremarkable 16.57 deg C summer; the snowman was wrong. 2003 - second shortest at 5.70 min - was followed by a record-shattering 21.67 deg C summer; the snowman was right but, MeteoSwiss says, by chance. 2022 burned for 37.98 min and the summer hit 20.40 deg C (a record); the snowman was wrong. 2023 burned for a record 57 min, then the summer was 20.07 deg C (a record); the snowman was wrong. Even 2025 burned for 26.50 min, a slow time, and was followed by a 19.60 deg C record summer. Across the eight celebrity years (1974, 2003, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023, 2025), the folk rule is right once.

ana_10.label: Long-run trend in Swiss-Plateau summer temperature
ana_10.content: Linear regression over all 67 years gives a slope of +0.0415 deg C per year, r = 0.675, p = 3.81e-10 - a strong, highly significant warming trend. Implied 100-year warming is 4.15 deg C. Comparing the first 30 years on record (1923-1987) with the last 30 years (1995-2025), mean summer temperature rises from 16.67 deg C to 18.53 deg C - a 1.86 deg C gap. So while the snowman fails to predict whether any individual summer is hot, the underlying summers are getting hotter on a schedule.

ana_11.label: Long-run trend in Boeoegg burn duration (and decadal pattern)
ana_11.content: The headline regression of duration on year is statistically inconclusive: slope +0.0756 min/year, r = 0.136, p = 0.281. But the decadal medians tell a clearer story than the slope. The 1950s-60s averaged 6-11 min burns, the 1970s-80s averaged 17-21 min, the 1990s and 2000s drifted back down to roughly 10-15 min, and the 2020s have so far averaged 33.6 min - more than five times the 1950s. This is the period MeteoSwiss flags as having loose, smoldering pyres rather than a meaningful climate signal.

data_table.description: Decadal mean and median burn duration (count of years per decade)

ana_12.label: Year-by-year duration vs summer T (full scatter table)
ana_12.content: All 65 paired (year, duration, summer T, record) observations are stored in this finding for the main scatter chart that visualizes the failure of the folk rule. Visually, the cloud is unstructured: short burns appear in cool years (1956, 1968) and hot years (2003, 2017); long burns appear in cool years (1923, 1988, 1970) and hot years (2022, 2023). Record summers (n=10 with non-null duration) sit at burn times ranging from 5.7 min to 57 min - the entire spread.

data_table.description: All 65 paired (year, duration, summer mean T, record) rows for the main scatter

ana_13.label: Record summers by decade
ana_13.content: Frequency of record summers (mean >= 19 deg C) by decade reveals an unmistakable acceleration. The 1920s through 1970s contain ZERO record summers across 22 observed years. The 1980s, 1990s and 2000s each contain just 1 record summer in 10 years (10%). The 2010s jump to 4 in 9 years (44.4%). The 2020s already sit at 4 record summers in 6 observed years (66.7%). What used to be a once-a-decade event is now the modal outcome - the climate signal is loud and obvious in the same dataset where the snowman signal is silent.

data_table.description: Record-summer count and percentage by decade

caveats.content: Two NA durations - 2020 (COVID-19 cancellation) and 2024 (storm cancellation, never occurred before in the modern festival's history) - are excluded from all duration-based analyses. The climate values for those years are still in the dataset and contribute to long-run trend statistics.

The duration column is heterogeneous in precision: pre-1980 entries are mostly rounded to whole minutes, while post-1990 entries are reported to two decimal places (typically derived from second-resolution timing). This may slightly inflate variance in the early decades but does not affect the central correlation results.

The dataset is sparse before 1952. Treat the 1923 row (60-minute burn, 16.67C summer) as a single data point not a representative pre-war sample. All correlation tests use the 65 burns that exist, with no imputation.
